attributes.title: Level 5

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the erase tool to smooth the outline of the cactus image, like removing the red pixels in this image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about how the pixels are positioned in the outline of the cactus image?

❓ Where might pixels be erased to remove any “jaggies” from the cactus outline?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 A “jaggy” is a break in a smooth line in an image. This often occurs when there are multiple pixels that are part of a line, rather than just one. Prompt the ninja to identify where multiple pixels are used in order to make sure the outline is 1 pixel wide. Have the ninja notice where pixels are connected linearly, rather than diagonally to create a smoother outline.

💡Point out to the ninja that a pixel art image outline should have clear lines. Have the ninja notice that the pixels in the cactus image should have clear, smooth edges to make it pop on the project screen.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by refining the image’s outline. 


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen, and notice the outline of the cactus0 image. 


Duplicate the cactus0 asset, then rename the new asset cactus1.


Notice the lines of the cactus and look for “jaggies”, or a break in a smooth line in the image. Use the erase tool to remove any double pixels from the outline. Make sure that pixels connect diagonally with other pixels in the outline.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the fill tool to add a base color, like green (7), inside of the cactus image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What base color(s) might be used in the cactus image?

❓ Why is it useful to add a base color to a pixel art image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Adding a base color provides a starting point for creating an image in pixel art. It adds definition before additional colors and different pixels are used to add depth to the image. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out different base colors to see which one might fit best. Because there are only 15 colors in MakeCode’s paint editor, colors often need to be strategically used to mimic what the object would look like in real life.
steps.instructions:
Add base colors to the cactus image!


Duplicate the cactus1 asset, then rename the new asset cactus2.


Use the fill tool to add a base color to the inside of the cactus image. Test out different base colors to see which one fits best.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you look for analogous colors in the color palette, then use them to draw vertical lines on the cactus image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is an analogous color? Why might it be used to add depth to an image?

❓ What color(s) might be used to add vertical lines to the cactus image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Analogous colors are groups of colors that are next to each other on the color wheel, or near each other in MakeCode’s color palette. Have the ninja identify which colors are analogous to the base color, then explore adding them to the cactus image to see which might match best.

💡 Encourage the ninja to tinker with where to place the vertical lines and what colors to use where, in order to add depth to the cactus image.
steps.instructions:
Add shading to the cactus image!


Duplicate the cactus2 asset, then rename the new asset cactus3.


In the paint editor, look for analogous colors, or colors that are near the base color of the cactus in the MakeCode palette and have similar colors. For example, if the base color of the cactus is green, different shades of blue (8 or 9) or teal (6) might be used to add shading.


Use the paint or line tools to draw vertical lines of alternating analogous colors inside the cactus image. This will create depth by adding shading to the image.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add polish to the cactus image with brown, tan, or white colors?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:                                

❓ What might you find on a cactus that can be added to the pixel art image? What colors might represent those features?

❓ Where might pixels be replaced to add polish to the cactus image to make it look less uniform?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Brainstorm with the ninja what features (e.g. spikes or bristles) are typically found on a cactus and what colors from the MakeCode color palette might best represent those features.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out replacing some of the pixels in the vertical line shading with either the base color or a color that represents a different feature.
steps.instructions:
Add polish to make the cactus image more lifelike!


Duplicate the cactus3 asset, then rename the new asset cactus4.


Look at the existing cactus image and consider what other features are typically found on a cactus (such as spikes or bristles) and what colors might be used to represent those features. Use the brown (14), tan (13), and white (1) colors to add polish around the cactus image. Tinker with removing some of the vertical line shading to create a more irregular design inside the cactus.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you smooth out the edges of the cactus image with dark purple and brown?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might dark purple and brown be used to smooth the edges of the cactus image?

❓ How does using different colors help soften the outline of an image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The existing black pixels in the outline create a strong contrast between the image and the background. This can work well if you want an image to stand out on the project screen. However, it can be useful to blend an image asset into the project screen naturally. By replacing the outline with softer colors like dark purple and brown, it creates a smoother transition from image asset to background.
steps.instructions:
Complete the cactus drawing by softening the edges!


Duplicate the cactus4 asset, then rename the new asset cactus5.


Look for areas of the outline where softer colors, such as dark purple (12) and brown (14), can be used to smooth the edges of the image to make them less “pointy”.


Add any other finishing touches to the cactus image before code is added to display it on the project screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you type assets, a dot operator, the asset type and the asset name inside 2 backticks `` for each element in the cactusImages array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you place the cactus image assets in the correct order in the cactusImages array?

❓ What background color might be used to display the cactus images on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the number of each image asset matches the corresponding index in the array so that each image adds onto the previous one.
steps.instructions:
Set the scene to display the cactus images on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add a // project initialization comment at the top. Below, declare a cactusImages array that stores the 6 cactus image assets.


Then, add a // project start comment and set the background color underneath.


Click ▶ to see the chosen background color appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add an xOffset value (25) with a spacing value (25), multiplied by the counter variable i like this: (25 + (25 * i)), to set each sprite’s x-position?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What values might you use to offset the sprites from the left side of the screen and to space out each sprite?

❓ How do the cactus images appear on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out their code to make sure the sprites are placed correctly on screen. Prompt them to consider which values should be added together and which should be multiplied to correctly position the images.

💡 Point out to the ninja that they made small updates to the cactus image in each iteration. Have them compare the first and last images to see how the drawing progressed over time.
steps.instructions:
Display the cactus image from each step of the process on screen!


Under // project start, use a for loop to create 6 sprites. Use the loop’s counter variable to select a different image from the cactusImages array, each time the loop runs.


Set the x-position of the sprites by adding a value to offset the left side of the screen with the spacing between each sprite, multiplied by the loop’s counter variable. Set the y-position to a coordinate in the middle of the screen.


Click ▶ to see each cactus image displayed on screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you update all 4 parameters in the runImageAnimation function so that the images in the cactusImages array continuously loop ?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might the runImageAnimation function be useful for showing multiple iterations of an image?

❓ What might the frameInterval and loop parameters be set to so that the images continuously rotate at a reasonable rate?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The runImageAnimation function can be useful for showing how an image changes over time. In this context, because the cactus image was slowly added onto, the image animation helps the user visualize how it transformed in each version.
steps.instructions:
Add image animation to show the progression across the cactus images!


Under // project start, create a new sprite with its image set to the first element of the cactusImages array. Position the sprite to appear above the 5 sprites created in the for loop.


Animate the sprite’s image to rotate through each of the elements in the cactusImages array. Update the frameInterval and loop parameters so that the images continuously cycle through.


Click ▶ to see the development of the custom cactus image on screen!

subgroups.title: Pixel Art Colors & Outlines
subgroups.introduction: Create and refine an original pixel art image that contains analogous colors and a smooth outline

validationItems.text: Store 6 unique cactus image assets in a cactusImages array.
Place the 6 cactus images on screen using a for loop.
Animate a sprite that cycles through the 6 images.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about creating original pixel art images. You’ll be able to take the strategies you learn in this level to create detailed assets in future projects! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: Pixel Artist
badges.description: Use a variety of pixel art techniques to create original pixel art assets to be used in a project.

badges.title: Work of Art
badges.description: Create and refine original pixel art images in the MakeCode paint editor.

badges.title: Neat n’ Tidy
badges.description: Create smooth outlines by removing jaggies in a pixel art image.

badges.title: Color Wheel
badges.description: Use analogous or complementary colors to modify the level of contrast in a pixel art image.

badges.title: Depth Perception
badges.description: Add highlights and shadows to make a pixel art image look realistic.

badges.title: I’m Dithering Away!
badges.description: Use dithering to ease the transition between colors in a pixel art image.

badges.title: Up to Scale
badges.description: Create and refine multiple sizes of a pixel art image.
